sheets.heading: Crisis Management Life Cycle — 3 Phases
sheets.text:
Crisis Management Life Cycle — 3 Phases

The life cycle of crisis management is broadly divided into:

PRE-CRISIS → DURING CRISIS → POST-CRISIS

Phase Key focus Pre-crisis Prevention / mitigation, preparedness, risk reduction During crisis Immediate response, rescue, relief and crisis handling Post-crisis Recovery → Rehabilita on → Reconstruc on

Disaster Management — 4 Phases

Mitigation

Objective: Reduce disaster risk and minimise future losses.

Key points:

• Risk assessment → Mi ga on

• Non-structural mitigation → community awareness and educa on programmes.

• Cyclone mitigation → planting trees along coastal areas.

• Earthquake mitigation → reframing building-construction guidelines and implementation.

Preparation

Objective: Be ready before the disaster occurs.

Includes:

• Preparedness planning

• Warning systems

• Evacuation arrangements

• Community preparedness

• Emergency resources and coordination

Response

• Objective: Immediate action during/just after the disaster.

• Community is usually the first responder.

• Urban response involves civic authorities + fire brigade + local police, while the district administration has the basic responsibility, with the Collector playing a pivotal role.

• In the post-disaster scenario, the operation that plays a major role is Search and Rescue

Recovery

• Objective: Restore normal life and reduce future vulnerability.

• Post-crisis stage: Recovery → Rehabilita on → Reconstruc on

DROUGHT MANAGEMENT

Historical development

• Arthashastra — 4th century B.C.: devoted a section to mitigation measures to combat famines.

• After Independence → drought relief works undertaken in severely affected areas.

• Green Revolution — late 1960s → necessity for famine-relief work declined.

• A holistic drought-management programme was taken up as Drought Prone Areas Programme (DPAP).

• Disaster Management Act — 2005 → na onal-level disaster-management legislation.

sheets.heading: Hailstorm
sheets.text:
Hailstorm

Point Fact Definition Precipitation in the form of ice pellets (hailstones) formed in strong

thunderstorms Nature Localised, short-duration, high-intensity weather hazard Formation Strong updrafts in cumulonimbus clouds freeze raindrops; repeated layering

increases size Season in India Mainly Pre-monsoon (March–May) and Winter; rare during monsoon India’s Frequency High – among countries with frequent moderate to severe hail events

Vulnerable Regions in India

Factor Details Atmospheric Strong convective instability + abundant moisture + strong updrafts Synoptic Western Disturbances, wind discontinuity lines Topographic Plateaus and hilly regions enhance convection Climate Change Increasing frequency and intensity of extreme convective events

sheets.heading: Cloudburst
sheets.text:
Cloudburst

Cloudburst Fact Type/context Sudden extreme rainfall event → conceptually linked to rapid-onset

disasters Flood connection Heavy rainfall can contribute to flooding Landslide connection Prolonged rainfall → heavy landslides Landslide consequence Landslide can block rivers → downstream havoc Flood management Flood forecasting + warning + disaster preparedness Urban vulnerability Poor drainage, urbanization and poor planning aggravate flooding

Point Fact Definition (IMD) Extremely intense rainfall area of ≈ 20–30 sq km

of ≥ 100 mm (10 cm) in one hour over a small

Nature Highly localised, short-duration extreme weather event Common Association Often accompanied by thunderstorms; triggers flash floods & landslides Altitude Preference Mostly occurs between 1,000–2,500 m in mountainous regions

Factor Explanation Orographic Lifting Warm moist air forced to rise rapidly over steep mountain slopes Atmospheric Instability Strong convection leads to towering cumulonimbus clouds Moisture Availability High moisture content in monsoon air masses Sudden Release When updrafts weaken, accumulated water falls intensively

Region Key States Why Vulnerable? Himalayan Region

Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, J\&K, Ladakh, Sikkim

Steep slopes + orographic effect + monsoon Western Ghats Parts of Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra Intense monsoon windward side

rainfall on

Other Occasional events in plains (rare) Localised convection

Question Answer IMD definition of cloudburst ≥ 100 mm rainfall in 1 hour over ≈ 20–30 sq km Most vulnerable region Himalayan states (Uttarakhand, Himachal, J\&K) Main trigger mechanism Orographic lifting of moist air Major secondary hazards Flash floods + Landslides Forecasting challenge Extremely difficult due to highly localised nature Key forecasting tool Doppler Weather Radar + Nowcasting Related famous events Leh (2010), Kedarnath (2013), recent Himalayan events

climatological average during the winter season Season in India Mainly November to March (peak impact: December–February) Nodal Agency for Forecasting India Meteorological Department (IMD) Key Guidelines NDMA Guidelines on Cold Wave and Frost (2021) Status Notified disaster eligible for assistance under SDRF/NDRF
